Text:
In a healthy, full-term newborn, four reflexes are present at birth:

{{c1::Moro (startle)}}

{{c1::palmar grasp}}

{{c1::rooting}}

{{c1::sucking}}
Back Extra:
Ex: an object placed in the newborn's palm makes the hand close around it — that is the palmar grasp; stroking the lips prompts the baby to latch on — that is the sucking reflex.

Cue: rooting and sucking are the two reflexes that serve feeding.

Text:
Name the newborn reflex from how it presents:

The arms fly open wide and the fingers spread, as if grabbing at something = the {{c1::Moro}} reflex

Something touches the cheek and the head turns toward the touch = the {{c1::rooting}} reflex
Back Extra:
Cue: the Moro reflex is more often called the startle reflex.

Why: the newborn nervous system is well established at birth but not yet mature, which is why a healthy, full-term infant already produces these responses reliably.

Text: {{c1::Fontanelles::structures}} are the {{c2::flexible fibrous gaps between cranial bones}}, and they let the newborn's head {{c3::change shape}} as it passes through the narrow birth canal.
Back Extra: Why: in the months after birth the cranial bones grow together and fuse into a unified, rigid structure, so a fontanelle is a temporary finding.

Text:
The fontanelles do not close at the same age:

Posterior fontanelle → closes by {{c1::the third month}}

Anterior fontanelle → closes between {{c1::9 and 18 months}}
Back Extra: Cue: the anterior fontanelle stays open far longer than the posterior one, so beyond early infancy it is the only fontanelle left to assess.

Text: In an infant with an open fontanelle, a {{c1::depressed::depressed or bulging}} fontanelle may indicate {{c2::dehydration}}, whereas a {{c1::bulging::depressed or bulging}} fontanelle often signals {{c2::increased intracranial pressure}}.
Back Extra:
Mnemonic: a sunken fontanelle is a low tank — think fluid loss.

Pitfall: a fontanelle reads this way only while it is still open, so the sign is gone once it has closed.

Text: Teething (baby teeth breaking through the gums) can be {{c1::painful}} and is sometimes accompanied by a {{c1::low-grade}} fever.
Back Extra: Pitfall: teething accounts only for a low-grade fever, so a higher fever in an infant is not explained by teething.
